# Subacute thyroiditis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Thyroid and parathyroid gland disorders > Subacute thyroiditis*

[Original Article Link](/library/dg0o82)

---

## Summary

Subacute thyroiditis is a group of conditions characterized by transient inflammation of the <u>thyroid</u> that classically progresses through a triphasic course: <u>thyrotoxicosis</u>, followed by <u>hypothyroidism</u>, and eventually a return to a <u>euthyroid</u> state. The two main subtypes are <u>subacute granulomatous thyroiditis</u> (<u>de Quervain thyroiditis</u>), often preceded by a viral infection and manifests with a painful <u>goiter</u>, and <u>subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis</u> (silent or <u>painless thyroiditis</u>), which includes <u>postpartum thyroiditis</u>, and is caused by autoimmune disease and certain medications. Symptoms are generally milder than in other forms of <u>thyrotoxicosis</u> and <u>hypothyroidism</u>. Diagnostic studies reveal <u>thyroid</u> dysfunction and features of <u>destructive thyroiditis</u> on imaging (i.e., low or no <u>iodine</u> uptake on <u>RAIU measurement</u>, decreased vascularity on <u>thyroid ultrasound with Doppler</u>). In <u>subacute granulomatous thyroiditis</u>, <u>inflammatory markers</u> are elevated during the thyrotoxic phase, whereas they remain normal in <u>subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis</u>. Treatment is often unnecessary as <u>thyroid</u> dysfunction is typically mild. <u>Beta blockers</u> may be used to manage <u>thyrotoxicosis</u> symptoms, and <u>NSAIDs</u> or <u>prednisone</u> to manage the <u>pain</u> in <u>subacute granulomatous thyroiditis</u>. During the hypothyroid phase, <u>levothyroxine replacement</u> is indicated for <u>symptomatic hypothyroidism</u> and certain patients with <u>postpartum thyroiditis</u>. Most patients (over 80%) become <u>euthyroid</u> within a year, though recurrence is possible, and some may develop permanent <u>hypothyroidism</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (3:1)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 30–50 years





References:[[1]](/library/U30b3f)[[2]](/library/o600NS)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Overview

Subacute thyroiditis is characterized by transient patchy inflammation of the <u>thyroid gland</u>. Depending on the underlying cause, one of two types of histological changes is seen.

| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br>Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis <br>(also known as <u>giant cell thyroiditis</u>, <u>de Quervain thyroiditis</u>, and subacute thyroiditis) | <br>Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis (also known as <u>painless thyroiditis</u> and <u>silent thyroiditis</u>) |
| Etiology | <br>* Viral infections<br><br>* <u>Mumps</u><br><br>* <u>Coxsackie virus</u><br><br>* <u>Influenza virus</u><br><br>* <u>Echovirus</u><br><br>* <u>Adenovirus</u><br><br>* <u>COVID-19</u> [[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)[[6]](/library/ZhdZcp0)<br><br> | <br><br>* Autoimmune disease  [[7]](/library/ZIYZYq)<br><br>* <u>Postpartum thyroiditis</u> (autoimmune-mediated) [[5]](/library/msYVvq)<br><br>* Drug-induced thyroiditis<br><br>* α-<u>interferon</u><br><br>* <u>Lithium</u><br><br>* <u>Interleukin-2</u><br><br>* <u>Tyrosine kinase inhibitors</u><br><br>* <u>Amiodarone</u>  [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)<br><br><br> |

| Pathology | <br><br>* Damaged follicular cells<br><br>* <u>Multinucleated giant cells</u><br><br>* <u>Granulomas</u><br><br>* <u>Fibrosis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Damaged follicular cells<br><br>* <u>Lymphocytic</u> infiltration  [[7]](/library/ZIYZYq)<br><br><br> |
| Management | <br><br>* Diagnosis is confirmed on clinical history, <u>TFTs</u>, <u>inflammatory markers</u>, and <u>thyroid</u> imaging.<br><br>* Treatment is often unnecessary as <u>thyroid</u> dysfunction is mild. <br><br>* Thyrotoxic phase: <u>beta blockers</u><br><br>* Hypothyroid phase: <u>levothyroxine replacement</u><br><br>* Monitor <u>TFTs</u> every 4–8 weeks until <u>euthyroid</u>.<br><br><br> |  |

---

## Pathophysiology

Subacute thyroiditis classically has a triphasic clinical course. The duration of each phase may vary (see “Clinical features”).



1. * Thyrotoxic phase: caused by damage to follicular cells and the release of preformed colloid (stored <u>thyroid hormones</u>)
2. * Hypothyroid phase: caused by depletion of preformed colloid and impaired synthesis of new <u>thyroid hormones</u> as a result of damage to follicular cells
3. * <u>Euthyroid</u> phase: <u>thyroid</u> function recovers; pathological changes are no longer visible in the <u>thyroid gland</u>.




> [!TIP]
> The classic triphasic course occurs in approximately 30% of patients. Some may experience only the thyrotoxic phase, while others may go through only the hypothyroid phase.

---

## Clinical features

### <u>Prodrome</u> [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[6]](/library/ZhdZcp0)




* Can occur in patients with <u>subacute granulomatous thyroiditis</u>

* Consists of nonspecific symptoms (<u>malaise</u>, fatigue, low-grade <u>fever</u>) often preceded by an <u>upper respiratory tract infection</u>





### <u>Goiter</u> [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)




* <u>Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis</u>

* Painful, diffuse, firm <u>goiter</u>

* <u>Pain</u> may radiate to the <u>jaw</u> and <u>ears</u>

* <u>Pain</u> is exacerbated with <u>swallowing</u>, <u>coughing</u>, and neck movement

* <u>Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis</u>: painless <u>goiter</u>





![Surface anatomy of the thyroid gland](media/upv0dosb3jon9nkeqmmihw0b.jpg)

Surface anatomy of the thyroid gland




> [!NOTE]
> De Quervain thyroiditis is a common cause of <u>thyroid</u> <u>pain</u>. [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)




### Thyrotoxic phase [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)




* Manifests with <u>clinical features of hyperthyroidism</u>

* <u>Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis</u>

* Occurs in ∼ 50% of patients

* Lasts 3–6 weeks

* <u>Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis</u>

* Occurs in up to 20% of patients

* Lasts 3–4 months





### Hypothyroid phase [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)




* Manifests with <u>clinical features of hypothyroidism</u>

* Occurs in ∼ 30% of patients

* Typically lasts ≤ 6 months; permanent in ∼ 15% of individuals

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)[[6]](/library/ZhdZcp0)




* Obtain a comprehensive clinical history and perform a thorough <u>physical examination</u>.

* Evaluate for clinical signs of <u>thyroid</u> dysfunction.

* Assess <u>thyroid</u> size, symmetry, nodularity, and tenderness to palpation.

* Evaluate for an underlying cause, including performing a thorough <u>medication review</u>.

* See “<u>Overview of subacute thyroiditis</u>” for expected findings.

* Obtain <u>thyroid function tests</u> (<u>TFTs</u>).

* In patients with <u>thyrotoxicosis</u>, obtain:  [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[8]](/library/dTbopG)

* <u>Thyroid</u> imaging

* <u>Inflammatory markers</u> (in patients with a painful <u>thyroid</u>)

* Consider additional studies as needed to rule out differential diagnoses; see:

* <u>Diagnostic workup for hyperthyroidism</u>

* <u>Diagnostic workup for hypothyroidism</u>





> [!TIP]
> Screen <u>TFTs</u> every 3–6 months in patients taking medications associated with <u>drug-induced thyroiditis</u>. [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)




### <u>TFTs</u> [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[6]](/library/ZhdZcp0)




* Thyrotoxic phase: : ↓ <u>TSH</u>, ↑ T<sub>3</sub> and T<sub>4</sub>, ↑ <u>thyroglobulin</u>

* Hypothyroid phase: ↓ T<sub>3</sub> and T<sub>4</sub>, ↑ <u>TSH</u>





> [!TIP]
> Compared to <u>thyrotoxicosis</u> in other conditions (e.g., <u>Graves disease</u>), the <u>thyroid</u> dysfunction is mild and the T<sub>3</sub>:T<sub>4</sub> <u>ratio</u> is lower in subacute thyroiditis. See “<u>Overview of thyroid function tests</u>.” [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)




### <u>Inflammatory markers</u> [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)




* Indication: initial evaluation in individuals with a painful <u>goiter</u>

* Findings [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)

* <u>Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis</u>: ↑ <u>ESR</u> (> 50 mm/hour), ↑ <u>CRP</u>, ↑ <u>WBC</u> during the thyrotoxic phase

* <u>Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis</u>: normal values





### <u>Thyroid</u> imaging [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)[[8]](/library/dTbopG)




#### <u>RAIU measurement</u>




* Indication: evaluation of <u>thyrotoxicosis</u> of unknown cause in nonpregnant adults

* Findings: minimal or no uptake of <u>radioactive iodine</u> throughout the <u>thyroid gland</u>





![Thyroid scintigraphy](media/riwo5p37q47dmr4mc8ilyngp.jpg)

Thyroid scintigraphy

![Subacute thyroiditis](media/rxvg29154kx70nqmpfbj30kc.jpg)

Subacute thyroiditis




#### <u>Thyroid ultrasound with Doppler</u>




* Indication: : evaluation of <u>thyrotoxicosis</u> of unknown cause in pregnant or lactating individuals

* Findings: <u>thyroid</u> with heterogeneous <u>hypoechoic</u> regions and decreased vascularity





![Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain thyroiditis)](media/a3m6t5abvqvzbu5yv21txeyg.jpg)

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain thyroiditis)

![Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (De Quervain thyroiditis)](media/fjt612p110tp09pg4q7n62ev.jpg)

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (De Quervain thyroiditis)




### Additional studies




#### <u>Thyroid antibodies</u> [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[9]](/library/QD0uVR)




* Indications: not routinely indicated; consider to rule out differential diagnoses

* Findings

* <u>TRAbs</u>: negative

* <u>Anti-TPO antibodies</u>: positive in 50% of patients with <u>subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis</u>  [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[9]](/library/QD0uVR)[[10]](/library/13c2hX0)

* <u>Anti-Tg antibodies</u>: may be positive during the thyrotoxic phase  [[11]](/library/wSdhbp0)[[12]](/library/7Qd4xp0)





#### <u>Fine-needle aspiration biopsy</u>




* Indications [[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)

* Diagnostic uncertainty

* Suspected <u>neoplasm</u>

* Suspected <u>acute suppurative thyroiditis</u> (e.g., high <u>fever</u>, <u>leukocytosis</u>, <u>cervical lymphadenopathy</u>)

* Findings [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)

* <u>Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis</u>: <u>granulomatous inflammation</u>, <u>multinucleated giant cells</u>

* <u>Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis</u>: <u>lymphocytic</u> infiltration, sparse <u>germinal centers</u>





![Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis](media/pbhwfkf1ej7bp1wik164b6u3.jpg)

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis

## Treatment

### General principles [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)[[5]](/library/msYVvq)




* Subacute thyroiditis is a <u>self-limited</u> disease and <u>thyroid</u> dysfunction is typically mild.

* Management is symptomatic.

* Thyrotoxic phase: <u>beta blockers</u>, <u>NSAIDs</u>, <u>corticosteroids</u> as needed

* <u>Symptomatic hypothyroidism</u>: <u>levothyroxine replacement</u> until <u>thyroid</u> function recovers

* Regular follow-up and <u>TFTs</u> are necessary to monitor for changes in <u>thyroid</u> function.

* For management of <u>postpartum thyroiditis</u>, see “Special patient groups.”





### Thyrotoxic phase




* Do not administer <u>antithyroid drugs</u> (e.g., <u>methimazole</u>).  [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)[[6]](/library/ZhdZcp0)

* Initiate symptomatic management as needed, e.g.:

* <u>Symptomatic treatment for thyrotoxicosis</u> (e.g., <u>beta blockers</u>)  [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[5]](/library/msYVvq)

* <u>Analgesia</u> for patients with <u>pain</u> from <u>subacute granulomatous thyroiditis</u>  [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)

* Mild <u>pain</u>: <u>NSAIDs</u>, e.g., <u>ibuprofen</u> (see “<u>Oral analgesics</u>” for dosages)

* Moderate, severe, or refractory <u>pain</u> : <u>corticosteroids</u>, e.g., <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)

* <u>Drug-induced thyroiditis</u>: Consider discontinuing medication in consultation with a specialist.  [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)

* Monitor <u>thyroid</u> function every 2–4 weeks. [[13]](/library/kIYm1q)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Antithyroid drugs</u> are ineffective for subacute thyroiditis. [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)




### Hypothyroid phase




* Treatment is usually unnecessary as symptoms are typically mild or absent. [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)

* Patients with <u>overt hypothyroidism</u>

* Start <u>levothyroxine replacement</u>.  [[13]](/library/kIYm1q)

* Treatment duration is normally 3–6 months, but lifelong therapy may be required.  [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)

* Monitor <u>TFTs</u> 4–8 weeks after: [[5]](/library/msYVvq)[[14]](/library/meXVzC)

* Treatment initiation

* Dosage changes

* Cessation of therapy

* See also “<u>Management of hypothyroidism</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> In most cases, subacute thyroiditis is <u>self-limited</u>, but some patients experience recurrence, and permanent <u>hypothyroidism</u> occurs in ∼ 15% of patients. [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)

---

## Prognosis

* Most cases self-resolve within 12 months. [[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)

* Permanent <u>hypothyroidism</u> occurs in ∼ 15% of individuals. [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)

* Recurrence occurs in:

* Up to 4% of patients with <u>subacute granulomatous thyroiditis</u> [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)

* 5–10% of patients with <u>subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis</u>  [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)

---

## Special patient groups

### Postpartum thyroiditis [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[5]](/library/msYVvq)




* An autoimmune-mediated <u>destructive thyroiditis</u> that occurs within 12 months of the end of <u>pregnancy</u>

* Affects ∼ 5–10% of pregnant individuals [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)

* Most prevalent in individuals with: [[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)

* Personal or family history of <u>autoimmune thyroid disease</u> [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)

* <u>Type 1 diabetes</u>

* History of <u>postpartum thyroiditis</u>  [[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)





#### Clinical features [[5]](/library/msYVvq)




* Similar to clinical features of <u>subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis</u> in nonpostpartum patients

* Features manifest within 1–12 months of delivery or spontaneous or <u>induced abortion</u> [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[5]](/library/msYVvq)

* <u>Hyperthyroidism</u> usually occurs 1–6 months postpartum

* <u>Hypothyroidism</u> develops 3–12 months postpartum.  [[5]](/library/msYVvq)

* May be associated with <u>postpartum depression</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Hypothyroidism symptoms</u> are more common than <u>hyperthyroidism symptoms</u>, which are typically mild or absent in individuals with <u>postpartum thyroiditis</u>. [[5]](/library/msYVvq)




> [!TIP]
> Screen patients with <u>depression</u>, including <u>postpartum depression</u>, for <u>thyroid</u> dysfunction. [[5]](/library/msYVvq)




#### Diagnostics [[5]](/library/msYVvq)




The diagnostic workup is similar to <u>diagnostics for subacute thyroiditis</u> in nonpostpartum patients.




* In patients with <u>thyrotoxicosis</u>, the following tests are recommended to differentiate <u>postpartum thyroiditis</u> from <u>Graves' disease</u>. [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)[[5]](/library/msYVvq)

* Total T3 and total T4

* <u>TRAb</u>  [[4]](/library/zy1r3j0)

* Consider <u>thyroid</u> imaging.  [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[5]](/library/msYVvq)

* See “<u>Postpartum thyroiditis vs. Graves disease</u>” for findings.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>RAIU measurement</u> is contraindicated in <u>pregnancy</u> and lactation. If <u>RAIU measurement</u> is necessary during lactation, <u>iodine</u>-123 or <u>technetium-99m</u> should be used, and patients are advised to pump and discard <u>breast milk</u> for 3–5 days afterward. [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[5]](/library/msYVvq)




#### Differential diagnosis




<u>Postpartum thyroiditis</u> is the most common cause of <u>hyperthyroidism</u> in the <u>postpartum period</u>, but the <u>incidence</u> of <u>Graves disease</u> is 3–4 times higher postpartum than in the nonpostpartum period. [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[5]](/library/msYVvq)




| <br>Postpartum thyroiditis vs. Graves disease [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[5]](/library/msYVvq)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Postpartum thyroiditis</u> | <u>Graves disease</u> |
| Onset | <br>* Usually < 3 months after the end of <u>pregnancy</u><br><br> | <br>* Commonly > 6 months after delivery<br><br> |
| <u>Clinical features of Graves disease</u> | <br>* Absent<br><br> | <br>* Present<br><br> |
| <u>TSH receptor antibodies</u> | <br>* Typically negative  [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[5]](/library/msYVvq)<br><br> | <br>* Typically positive<br><br> |
| <br>T3:T4 <u>ratio</u> [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)<br> | <br>* < 20<br><br> | <br>* > 20<br><br> |
| <br><u>Thyroid ultrasound with Doppler</u> [[8]](/library/dTbopG)<br> | <br>* Decreased blood flow<br><br> | <br>* Increased blood flow<br><br> |
| <br><u>RAIU measurement</u> <br> | <br>* Reduced uptake<br><br> | <br>* Normal or increased uptake<br><br> |





#### Treatment [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)[[5]](/library/msYVvq)




Similar to <u>treatment of subacute thyroiditis</u> in nonpostpartum patients with the following modifications:




* Symptomatic <u>thyrotoxicosis</u>

* Use <u>propranolol</u> or <u>metoprolol</u> at the lowest effective dose in lactating patients.

* Monitor <u>TSH</u> every 4–8 weeks to screen for the onset of <u>hypothyroidism</u>.

* Hypothyroid phase

* Consider <u>levothyroxine replacement</u> in patients who:

* Have <u>overt hypothyroidism</u>

* Are <u>breastfeeding</u>

* Are trying to conceive

* Have a <u>TSH</u> level > 10 mIU/L [[3]](/library/8zaOuM)

* Continue replacement for 12 months and then gradually taper dosing.

* Monitor <u>TSH</u> every 6–8 weeks and adjust dosing accordingly.

* Long-term follow-up: Annual <u>TSH</u> testing is recommended for all patients to screen for permanent <u>hypothyroidism</u>.  [[5]](/library/msYVvq)





> [!TIP]
> Advise patients with <u>hypothyroidism</u> who are not on <u>levothyroxine</u> therapy to use <u>contraception</u> until <u>euthyroidism</u> is achieved. [[5]](/library/msYVvq)
